title: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and the ischaemic diabetic foot
subtitle: Drain sepsis first, then stage with WIfI and revascularise

sources.org: European Society for Vascular Surgery, Society for Vascular Surgery and World Federation of Vascular Societies
sources.title: Global Vascular Guidelines on the Management of Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia
The SVS Lower Extremity Threatened Limb Classification System: risk stratification based on Wound, Ischemia, and foot Infection (WIfI)

sources.org: International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot (IWGDF), ESVS and SVS
sources.title: The intersocietal IWGDF, ESVS, SVS guidelines on peripheral artery disease in people with diabetes mellitus and a foot ulcer

red_flags.text: A diabetic foot with spreading cellulitis, crepitus, a fluctuant swelling or systemic sepsis. Infection with ischaemia destroys a foot in hours; this is a surgical emergency.
Ischaemic rest pain at night relieved by hanging the foot over the bed, or tissue loss that has not healed in two weeks.
Dry gangrene that has become wet, or new pain in a previously neuropathic painless foot.
A normal or high ankle-brachial index in a diabetic or renal patient with a non-healing wound. Calcified arteries give a falsely reassuring reading.
Sudden worsening in a limb with known chronic disease: acute-on-chronic ischaemia, which needs the acute limb pathway.

do_now.text: Infected ischaemic foot: urgent drainage of abscess and debridement of necrotic infected tissue, together with broad-spectrum antibiotics per local protocol, before revascularisation. Sepsis control comes first.
Refer every patient with suspected CLTI to a vascular specialist for assessment of revascularisation. Do not plan a major amputation without it.
In a person with diabetes and a foot ulcer, consider urgent imaging and revascularisation when toe pressure is below 30 mmHg or TcPO2 below 25 mmHg.
Offload the wound and protect the heel today. Pressure on an ischaemic heel makes a new ulcer in a day.

assess.text: Stage the limb with WIfI: Wound, Ischaemia and foot Infection, each graded 0 to 3. The combined stage predicts amputation risk and benefit from revascularisation.
Measure ankle and toe pressures. GVG haemodynamic markers of CLTI include ankle pressure below 50 mmHg, ABI below 0.4, toe pressure below 30 mmHg or TcPO2 below 30 mmHg.
Grade chronic disease severity for the record and for trend.
Probe the ulcer to bone and examine the whole foot, including between the toes and the heel. Probe-to-bone positive raises osteomyelitis.
Assess patient risk: cardiac, renal and frailty status, life expectancy, and ambulatory function. This is the P of the GVG PLAN framework.

investigate.text: Arterial duplex as the first anatomical study; CT or MR angiography, or catheter angiography, to plan revascularisation.
Plain radiograph of the foot for gas, foreign body and osteomyelitis; MRI where osteomyelitis is uncertain.
Deep tissue or bone samples for culture at debridement, not superficial swabs.
FBC, CRP, U&E, HbA1c, glucose and lipids. Vein mapping of the great saphenous vein when bypass is an option.

resuscitate.text: Treat sepsis with fluids, antibiotics per local protocol and glucose control while source control is arranged.
Start best medical therapy for every patient: antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin, blood pressure and glucose control, and smoking cessation.
Adequate analgesia for rest pain, which often needs opioids until revascularisation.

definitive.text: Revascularise suitable patients with CLTI to relieve pain, heal wounds and save the limb. Choose open bypass or endovascular treatment by the GVG PLAN framework: patient risk, limb stage and anatomical pattern.
For bypass, autologous vein, ideally the great saphenous vein, is the conduit of choice.
Aim for in-line pulsatile flow to the foot, and where possible to the angiosome of the wound, especially in the diabetic foot.
Minor amputation and debridement after revascularisation to achieve a healable foot; staged closure is often needed.
Primary major amputation for a non-salvageable foot, a non-ambulatory patient with a flexion contracture, or overwhelming sepsis. Decide the level by perfusion and function.

escalate.text: Multidisciplinary diabetic foot team: vascular, diabetes, podiatry, orthotics, microbiology and wound care.
Urgent same-day vascular review for the infected ischaemic foot; transfer if no vascular service.
Senior vascular review before any major amputation, documenting why revascularisation is not possible or not appropriate.

notes: In diabetes the ABI lies. Toe pressures and Doppler waveforms tell the truth about the foot.
Drain first, revascularise second, reconstruct third. Revascularising pus spreads it.
A healed foot needs blood, off-loading and infection control together. Any one missing and the wound does not close.
